To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the cost of prescribing for cardiovascular prevention in primary health care is rising, but the majority of prescribing is for drugs that are not effective for the prevention of coronary heart disease and that there are many opportunities to reduce prescribing costs by reducing waste in the system.

(i) prescribing of cardiovascular drugs in primary care is increasing; (ii) there is a lot more prescribing of cardiovascular drugs than is required for the management of the patients’ cardiovascular risk; (iii) the prescribing of cardiovascular drugs for the management of cardiovascular disease is not evidence based; (iv) there are many patients who are not being prescribed the cardiovascular drugs that they require; and (v) there are a lot of patients who are being prescribed cardiovascular drugs that they do not require.
the cost of cardiovascular drugs is rising and that the prescribing of drugs for the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease is increasing.

the cost of prescribing in primary care and how we can improve the cost effectiveness of prescribing in this setting.
